Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
401 AM EST Wed Nov 25 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
High Wind Warnings have been issued for the Blue Ridge
Mountains, western slopes of the Alleghenies, and St. Mary's
County. Wind Advisories fill out the remainder of the area. All
marine products have been upgraded to warnings as well. For
temperatures, brought down highs on Thanksgiving Day given the
cool northeasterly winds.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Seasonably cool today ahead of a powerful coastal low set
  to bring hazardous weather on Thanksgiving Day.

- 2) Drier conditions anticipated this weekend before additional
  precipitation chances return early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Seasonably cool today ahead of a powerful
coastal low set to bring hazardous weather on Thanksgiving Day.

A strong dome of Canadian high pressure currently stretches from
the Great Lakes into southern Quebec and New England. The
influence of this ridge axis extends all the way down into the
Florida Panhandle. Locally, the influence of this anticyclone
comes with rather chily temperatures. As of 08Z/3 AM, most spots
are in the 20s to near freezing, with spotty mid/upper 30s where
light breezes off the Chesapeake Bay are occurring. With current
dew points in the upper teens to mid 20s, there will be
additional room to cool off temperatures ahead of daybreak.

While skies are currently clear, high cirrus have begun to lift
north of I-64. Additionally, some marine stratus are expanding
westward from the Delmarva Peninsula. Such clouds have reached
far southern Maryland. Meanwhile, ahead of the potent 
Thanksgiving Day system, mid to high clouds will continue to 
expand northward into the Mid-Atlantic region today. This all
sets to the stages for a period of hazardous weather tonight 
into Thanksgiving Day.

There are two key components aloft to consider for this major
pattern change ahead. Multi-channel water vapor imagery depicts
an upper low spinning across the Dakotas. A separate feature off
to the south is currently pushing across the Ozarks while taking
an eastward track toward the Gulf Coast. This more southern
disturbance is the one that begins to gain latitude along the
southeastern U.S. coast while attaining a negative tilt. This
strengthening process will yield a series of deepening cyclone
centers along a wavy occluding frontal system. Based on late
November climatology, this trough exhibits highly anomalous
parameters which include its moisture content, wind fields, and
degree of low-level convergence. This high-impact system is
expected to impact the local area late tonight through
Thanksgiving Day.

The intense wind field extends all the way down to the surface
layer. Most guidance even shows 70 to 80 knot wind vectors down
to the 925-mb level. The main question is can any of the gusty
showers bring this intense wind field down to the surface.
Forecast soundings show ample stability in the lower atmosphere,
but a few rogue gusts appro5aching 65 to 75 mph are not out of
the question. With the strong winds in place, an array of High
Wind Warnings and Wind Advisories have been issued. These
generally cover the morning to afternoon hours on Thanksgiving
Day. Most of the region can expect sustained winds of 25 to 30
mph with gusts to around 50 to 55 mph. All wind products expire
by the late afternoon to near sunset. 

Besides the wind, a moderate to heavy area of rain lifts 
northward across the area. This first impacts the I-64 corridor 
in the 3-9 AM window, with I-66 around 5-11 AM, and finally 
I-70 by 6 AM-noon. Rain totals of 1 to 2 inches may fall as 
this activity pushes through. Some sensitive locations could see
spotty flooding issues if the higher amount is realized. Once 
this shifts activity lifts north of the Mason-Dixon Line,
precipitation turns more scattered in nature as the upper 
trough passes overhead. Amidst all the wind and rain, 
temperatures should be on the cooler side due to prevailing 
northeasterly winds. Expect highs in the 50s with mainly 40s 
west of the Blue Ridge. Heading into the night, thick low clouds
will hold temperatures in the upper 30s to 40s.

The upper low currently over the Dakotas eventually crosses the
region by early Friday. Ample lift underneath this feature will
bring some scattered showers on Friday morning. On the back side
of the trough, some upslope rain/snow showers are expected along
the Allegheny Front. It is not the most favorable wind direction
which is just south of the west. Perhaps an inch of snow is
possible across the higher peaks. For the entire area, winds 
remain elevated with gusts up to 25 to 35 mph, locally nearing 
45 mph in the mountains. The westerly component to the winds 
does help warm temperatures back into the 50s. Cyclonic 
gradients remain tight into Friday night as lows fall into the 
30s to low 40s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drier conditions anticipated this weekend before
additional precipitation chances return early next week.

A brief period of ridging in the immediate aftermath of the coastal 
low will bring clearing clouds and diminishing winds Saturday & 
into Sunday. Temperatures will remain seasonable during this period, 
with daytime highs in the 40s and 50s and overnight lows generally 
in the 30s. Winds temporarily shift west to southwest through the 
weekend, with gusts up to 25-35 mph Saturday afternoon and 15-25 
mph Sunday afternoon. 

Winds shift back northwesterly Monday, accompanied by increasing 
cloud cover as the upper-level pattern shifts back to troughing over 
the Ohio River Valley before shifting east. Temperatures likely 
remain seasonable during this period, but precipitation chances will 
increase again as this troughing moves through the Mid-Atlantic. 
There is some uncertainty still regarding when exactly this system 
will bring impacts to the region, but overall the general consensus 
seems to be to anticipate further precipitation in the Nov 30-Dec 
2 timeframe as potentially a couple disturbances move through. As 
drought has been creeping back into the region from the extended dry 
weather earlier this month, any flooding concerns will likely remain 
restricted to the coast from any onshore flow, but will continue to 
monitor QPF totals over the next several days.

&&

.AVIATION /07Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Canadian high pressure to the north will maintain VFR conditions
throughout the day, but with increasing clouds as the
Thanksgiving Day system develops along the Gulf Coast. Light
northerlies will give way to an increasing northeasterly wind.
Gusts this evening move into the 20 to 30 knot range before 
reaching 30 to 40 knots near sunrise. This come with the
northward push of moderate to heavy rains that will impact the
terminals in the 06Z-18Z window (earlier for KCHO and later for
KBWI and KMTN). A robust wind field brings low-level shear on
the order of 50 to 55 knots in the lowest 2,000 feet. IFR
conditions are likely much of Thanksgiving Day, although there
will be some breaks in the rain during the afternoon/evening
hours. Strong northeasterly winds persist into the afternoon
with a gradual downtick thereafter. However, expect continued
east to northeasterly wind gusts into the night with visibility
restrictions in place.

Winds turn west to southwesterly on Friday, but remain gusty in
nature. The forecast calls for afternoon gusts to around 25 to
30 knots, which may come with a few restrictions as scattered
showers accompany an upper low. Otherwise, expect a
stratocumulus deck to persist through the day. Winds diminish
slightly into Friday night.

VFR to MVFR conditions will return for Friday and Saturday as 
coastal/upper-level low pressure depart the region. Most terminals 
will remain dry, although LLWS will also remain an issue Friday 
morning into Friday afternoon and potentially again late 
Saturday into Sunday. VFR conditions will prevail Sunday under brief 
high pressure before sub-VFR conditions return with a series of low 
pressure systems early to mid next week. Winds stay gusty near 25-30 
knots Friday evening before diminishing some Saturday. Winds may 
briefly shift southerly Sunday before swinging northwesterly early 
next week.

&&

.MARINE...
A multi-period of hazardous marine conditions is expected 
across the region. Stout high pressure across New England is 
leading to a brisk northeasterly winds across the waterways. 
While some locations are not seeing advisory-caliber winds, a 
number of spots in the Chesapeake Bay are currently gusting 20 
to 25 knots. Small Craft Advisories go into effect for all 
waters this morning and will remain that way through the 
evening. Thereafter, have upgraded to Gale and Storm Warnings 
for tonight into Friday morning. The Storm Warnings are in 
effect for the more southern waters where gusts to around 50 to 
55 knots are possible. Elsewhere, gales will carry gusts of 40 
to 45 knots. This also includes high waves on the order of 3 to 
6 feet. Thereafter, winds shift to west to southwesterly for 
much of Friday. Given gradients remain tight, Small Craft 
Advisories will be needed given gusts up to 20 to 30 knots.

Wind gusts likely stay above at least SCA thresholds on Saturday 
before diminishing on Sunday. Winds could remain near-threshold 
levels Monday & Tuesday during the daytime before diminishing at 
night. Winds may briefly shift southerly Sunday before swinging 
northwesterly early next week.

&&

.TIDES/COASTAL FLOODING...
Intense low pressure will move up the coast, with very strong
(near record) high pressure to the north. This results in a
period of strong onshore flow. Tidal anomalies of two to three
feet are expected as a result, depending on the exact track and
strength of the low. Something around two feet above normal
would result in widespread minor tidal flooding, with moderate
in the favored vulnerable areas from Annapolis to Straits Point,
and perhaps DC/Alexandria. Anomalies closer to three feet could
result in more widespread moderate tidal flooding, with minor
even possible in spots that typically flood much less frequently
(i.e. shoreline in Cecil, Prince William, Prince Georges and
Fairfax Counties). The storm should move quickly enough to
preclude major flooding anywhere.

The heaviest rain may coincide with high tide around southern
Maryland, furthering the flooding risk due to drainage issues
along the coast with fresh plus tidal input on Thursday.

Winds shift around to the west and southwest Thursday night into
Friday, which isn't the most favorable for water to quickly 
evacuate the bay. Given the high astronomical tides (full moon 
occurred Tuesday/Nov 24), this could keep a risk of minor to
even moderate tidal flooding in the picture through Friday night.

&&
